name: spacta
description: Spacta — Pure-boundary architecture physically enforced by AST static verification
author: Ogatsuki
//exports: Two entry points, because the engine is two things and only one of them knows what React is.
`spacta/runtime` names no UI framework — that is the property `engine-portability` checks,
and shipping it as its own entry point is what makes the claim usable rather than merely
true. `spacta/react` is the binding adapter. An adopter on another view layer imports the
first and writes their own second.
The `.ts` source ships alongside `dist/` as the readable half — it is what an adopter opens
and what `engine-portability` walks; consumers get the compiled copy so nothing has to be
//bin: Three tools ship, and one deliberately does not. `verify`, `measure` and `garden` each take
a target path and read nothing but that target and this package — they work on anybody's
app. `tools/mutate.mjs` drives `replay/`, whose scenarios import the reference application
by relative path, so it measures this repository's gates and not an adopter's. Shipping it
would be shipping a tool that cannot run where it lands.
//files-replay: Named one by one rather than shipping `replay/` whole, and the line between them is the
point. These four name no application. The ones left behind — scenarios.mjs, crosscheck.mjs
and the two test files — import the reference app by relative path, so publishing them would
be publishing code that cannot run where it lands.
//files-docs: One rule, and it removes a whole class of broken link: **the package carries documents that
are read by machines, plus the two npm always shows a human — README and LICENCE. Nothing
else.** Everything a person reads at leisure lives in the repository, and the package points
there with an absolute URL rather than shipping a copy.
What that leaves in: `docs_AI-ONLY/SPACTA.md` (SKILL.md sends the agent to it by path),
`skills/**` and `garden/GARDENER.md` (the agent is told to read them by the tools' output).
What it takes out: CHANGELOG.md, verify/README.md and starter/README.md — prose for people,
80kB of it, none of it reachable from anything the package installs.
The rule is not a preference. The repository and the tarball are different trees, so a
relative link written in one is a dead link in the other; shipping only what the machines
read means there is almost nothing left that could hold such a link, and what remains is
checked — `tools/smoke-package.mjs` walks every installed document and fails on a relative
link with nothing behind it. Surveyed eight packages an adopter already has installed
(react, react-dom, next, typescript, eslint, @eslint/js, typescript-eslint, tailwindcss):
all eight ship README and LICENSE and nothing else. This is the convention, not a departure.
//peerDependencies: Both are optional, and for different reasons. `react` is needed only by `spacta/react`;
an adopter using the engine alone never resolves it. `typescript` is needed only by the
CLIs, which parse the target's AST — `verify.mjs` resolves it from the target project
first and from this package second, so a normal TypeScript app already satisfies it and
declaring it a hard dependency would put a compiler in every consumer's production tree.

scripts.//ci: What CI runs that needs nothing beside this repository. The behavioural gates are not here: they read the reference application, so they live in `replay` and `mutate` and run only where a checkout of it exists.
scripts.ci: npm run build && npm run verify && npm run measure && npm run garden && node tools/smoke-package.mjs
scripts.//replay: Needs a TypeScript-capable runtime (bun, deno, or node with type stripping): the scenarios import the reference app's core.ts directly. It also needs the engine built, because the harness drives dist/ rather than a copy of the source.
scripts.replay: npm run build && node replay/crosscheck.mjs && node replay/runtime.serialization.test.mjs && node replay/harness.selftest.mjs
